hint: What does post-increment evaluate to?

choices.text: The expression came out 0, which counts as failure
choices.why: Correct. `count++` yields the value before incrementing, and `(( ))` maps zero to a non-zero status.

choices.text: `count` had not been declared as an integer
choices.why: Arithmetic contexts treat any name as a number.
It is; the increment happened.
Statement-form `(( ))` is ordinary bash and is allowed.

prompt: A script needs an average with a decimal point. `$(( ))` cannot. Name the calculator it pipes to instead: `echo 'scale=2; 7/2' | ____`
hint: Two letters.

prompt: `p=/var/log/app.log`. Which spelling gives `app.log`?
hint: Remove the longest thing ending in a slash.

choices.why: That removes from the back and gives the directory.
Correct — this is `basename`, without a process.
A single `#` removes the shortest match, leaving `var/log/app.log`.
That removes the longest match from the back and leaves an empty string.

prompt: What is the difference between `${v-x}` and `${v:-x}`?
hint: One character, and one case.

choices.text: The first one assigns a value and the second does not
choices.why: Assigning is `${v:=x}`, which is a third spelling.

choices.text: The first is POSIX and the second is bash
choices.why: Both are POSIX and both work in dash.

choices.text: The colon makes an empty value count as missing
choices.why: Right, and that is the one you usually want.

choices.text: The colon makes the default a literal
choices.why: Defaults are expanded the same way in both.

prompt: `f=notes.tar.gz`. What does `${f%.*}` produce?
hint: A single `%` removes the shortest match.

choices.why: Correct — only the last extension goes, because the match is the shortest one.
That is `${f%%.*}`, or `${f%.tar.gz}` if you name the suffix.
Removing from the back leaves the front, not the back.
That would be `${f##*.}`.

prompt: Why is `name=${path##*/}` preferred over `name=$(basename "$path")`?
hint: Two reasons, and one of them shows up in a loop over ten thousand files.

choices.why: It is part of coreutils and is present everywhere you will meet.

choices.text: `basename` gets the answer wrong on nested paths
choices.why: It handles them correctly; the objection is elsewhere.

choices.text: The expansion keeps a trailing slash that `basename` drops
choices.why: Neither of them keeps one on a plain file path.

choices.text: It starts no process, and survives an odd filename
choices.why: Right — a name beginning with a dash is an option to `basename` and ordinary text to the expansion.

prompt: Match each expansion to its result.
hint: Two of them are about defaults.

pairs.right: how many characters v holds
stop with msg when v is unset or empty
replace every a with b
the value in lower case

right_distractors: replace the first a with b

prompt: Why `mktemp` rather than `/tmp/myscript.$$`?
hint: Think about two copies running at once, and about who else is on the machine.

choices.text: `$$` is not available in a script
choices.why: It is; it holds the shell's own process id.

choices.text: `mktemp` puts the file in memory instead of writing it to disk
choices.why: It creates an ordinary file, in an ordinary directory.

choices.text: A process id is guessable, so somebody could get there first
choices.why: Right. `mktemp` creates the file itself, in one step that cannot be raced.

choices.text: `$$` changes its value while the script is still running
choices.why: It stays the same for the life of the shell.

prompt: Where does `trap 'rm -rf "$work"' EXIT` belong in the file?
hint: What is the window you are trying to close?

choices.why: Correct. Anything between creating it and arming the trap is a gap where the script can die and leave it.

choices.text: At the very bottom, after the work
choices.why: A failing script does not reach the bottom, which is the case the trap is for.
There are usually several exits, and the error paths come earlier.

choices.text: Inside the cleanup function it calls
choices.why: The function would then have to be called to arm itself.

prompt: A script traps `INT` and exits 130 from the handler. It also traps `EXIT`. On Ctrl-C, which handlers run?
hint: An `exit` is still an exit.

choices.why: The `exit` in it is what fires the other one.
Right, and that is why cleanup belongs on `EXIT`: it is reached whichever way the script ends.
The signal handler is what caught the Ctrl-C in the first place.

choices.text: Neither, because Ctrl-C kills the shell outright
choices.why: That is `KILL`; `INT` is catchable, which is the point of trapping it.

prompt: Why is the trap command written in single quotes, as `trap 'rm -rf "$work"' EXIT`?
hint: When should `$work` be looked up?

choices.text: Double quotes are a syntax error there
choices.why: They parse fine; they just mean something else.

choices.text: Single quotes stop `rm` being run immediately
choices.why: Neither form runs it now; `trap` stores the text either way.

choices.text: The trap accepts just a single-quoted string
choices.why: It accepts any word, including a function name with no quotes at all.

choices.text: So `$work` is expanded when the trap fires
choices.why: Correct. With double quotes it is expanded at the moment the trap is set, which breaks if the value changes later.

prompt: `bash -n deploy.sh` reports a syntax error at line 40, the last line of the file. Where is the mistake likely to be?
hint: A shell cannot know which block you meant to close.

choices.text: On line 40, exactly where it says
choices.why: The end of file is where the shell ran out of input, not where the block opened.
The report is not off by one; it is at the end for a structural reason.

choices.text: Anywhere above, in a block that was never closed
choices.why: Right. A missing `fi`, `done`, `esac` or `}` always lands the complaint at the bottom.

choices.text: In a different file that this one sources at the top
choices.why: `-n` parses one file and does not follow a `source`.

prompt: `count=3` and `if [ $count > 5 ]` prints `many`, and a file called `5` appears. What did the `>` do?
hint: It is the same `>` you use everywhere else.

choices.text: Compared the two values as ordinary strings
choices.why: String comparison inside `[` is spelled `\>`, escaped.
Correct, and `[ 3 ]` asks whether `3` is a non-empty string, which is true.

choices.text: Been ignored as an unknown operator
choices.why: Nothing was ignored; a file appeared.

choices.text: Been read as part of the number `3`
choices.why: The number was never touched.

prompt: You set `PS4` at the prompt and `bash -x script.sh` still shows a plain `+`. What is missing?
hint: Which shell prints the trace?

choices.why: The `-x` on the command line already switched tracing on.

choices.text: A trailing space at the end of `PS4`
choices.why: The spacing changes how it looks, not whether it is used.
That is about how `echo` handles escapes.
Right. The trace is printed by the bash you are starting, and it only sees exported variables.

prompt: A nine-line script parses cleanly with `bash -n` and still has four bugs. Which tool finds them?
hint: It has a rule number for each one.

choices.why: Yes. It reads the script the way an experienced reviewer would, and does not get bored.
It shows what happened, which needs you to run the script first.
That echoes lines before running them, unexpanded.
Useful once you suspect a particular value, and it inspects nothing else.

prompt: Put the top of a well-built script in order.
trap: The trap goes after the thing it cleans up, not at the end of the file.

prompt: One line of a script reads `rm -rf $DEST/old`. Name the single worst thing that can happen.
hint: What is `$DEST` if the assignment three lines up had a typo?

choices.text: The command fails with a syntax error
choices.why: It is syntactically perfect, which is the problem.

choices.text: It deletes `/old` at the root of the disk
choices.why: Correct. An empty variable closes the path up, silently, and the command succeeds.

choices.text: `rm` refuses because the path is relative
choices.why: The path begins with a slash either way.

choices.text: The shell warns that the variable was empty
choices.why: Only `set -u` produces that warning, and the line does not have it.

prompt: Match each symptom to the setting that would have caught it.
hint: Three are `set` flags and one is a separate tool.

pairs.left: a typo'd variable name became an empty string
pairs.right: set -u

pairs.left: a failed command was followed by six more
pairs.right: set -e

pairs.left: a pipeline reported success after grep found nothing
pairs.right: set -o pipefail

pairs.left: a missing quote around a filename with a space
pairs.right: shellcheck

prompt: Which line safely passes every argument the script was given on to another command?
hint: Two arguments in should be two arguments out.

choices.why: Joined and then split again, so a value with a space is cut up.
That produces one argument containing all of them.
The quotes are what make `$@` keep its boundaries.
Correct. One quoted word per argument, whatever is inside them.

prompt: Turn a glob that matches nothing into zero iterations rather than one: `shopt -s ____`
hint: One word, eight letters.

prompt: A script counts lines into `total` inside `cat f | while read l; do total=$((total+1)); done` and `total` is 0 after. What is the smallest fix?
hint: Which side of the pipe is the loop on?

choices.text: `done < f`, dropping the `cat` and the pipe
choices.why: Correct. No pipe means no subshell, and it removes a process at the same time.
Exporting sends a value down to a child; it does not bring one back up.
The arithmetic was right; the trouble is where it happened.

choices.text: `local total` at the top of the script
choices.why: `local` is for functions, and it would change nothing here.

prompt: You need the directory a path points into, with no process started. Which one?
hint: The `%` operator removes from the back.

choices.why: That gives the filename — it is `basename`.
Right answer, wrong requirement: that starts a process.
Correct. Remove the shortest match ending at the last slash, and the directory is left.
The longest match from the back leaves an empty string on an absolute path.

prompt: Which of these are true of `[[ ]]` but not of `[ ]`?
hint: One of them is why `[ $x = y ]` breaks on an empty `x`.

choices.text: unquoted expansions are not split into words
choices.why: It is shell syntax, so the shell parses inside it rather than expanding into arguments.
`[[ $f == *.log ]]` is a pattern; `[ ]` compares the text it was handed.
`[` has no such operator.

choices.text: it exists in dash as well as bash
choices.why: It is a bash keyword, which is the one reason to still write `[ ]`.

choices.text: it can test whether a file is a directory
choices.why: Both do `-d`; the file tests are shared.

prompt: A function prints a progress line and returns a number. The caller gets both. Where should the progress line go?
hint: Command substitution captures one of the two streams.

choices.text: Into a variable the caller reads afterwards
choices.why: That is more machinery than the problem needs.
Correct. `$( )` captures standard output only, so the answer stays clean.

choices.text: Into a log file named in the function
choices.why: It works and takes the message away from whoever is watching.
Progress output is useful; it just belongs on the other stream.

prompt: Put these debugging steps in the order you should reach for them.
trap: Two of them do not need the script to run at all, and those come first.

prompt: Which of these stops a script under `set -e`?
hint: Three of the four are the holes.

choices.why: A condition is allowed to be false.
The failure is on the left of `||`, so you are handling it.

choices.text: a failing command inside a function used as a condition
choices.why: The suspension covers the whole call.

choices.text: `cp /etc/nothing /tmp/x` on a line of its own
choices.why: Correct — the plain case, and the one `-e` is actually for.

prompt: Ninety per cent of quoting bugs go away with one habit. Complete it, for the variable `f`: always write `____`
hint: Four characters.

prompt: An option parser reads `-t` and takes its value from `$2`. How many times must it `shift` for that branch?
hint: Count the words the branch used up.

choices.why: Correct — one for the flag and one for the value, which is why the branch has an extra `shift` of its own.

choices.text: Once, at the bottom of the loop
choices.why: That consumes the flag and leaves the value to be read as a target.

choices.text: Three times, to clear the whole option
choices.why: An option and a value are two words, not three.

choices.text: Zero times, since `$2` was read directly
choices.why: Reading a word does not remove it from the list.

prompt: Your script has grown to two hundred lines, parses JSON, and computes an average. What does that suggest?
hint: Three of bash's weak points are in that sentence.

choices.text: Break it into sourced function libraries
choices.why: That organises the code and leaves the arithmetic and the JSON where they were.
It fixes the fractions and neither of the other two.
Right. Structured data and real arithmetic are the two things bash is worst at, and two hundred lines is a cheap rewrite.
Worth doing anyway, and it does not address what the script is being asked to do.

prompt: `./tidy.sh` exits 1 on an error path and leaves no temporary file behind. What made that work?
hint: The exit was not the one the author was thinking about.

choices.text: The `rm` on the last line of the script
choices.why: An error path does not reach the last line.
Correct. `EXIT` fires on any exit, including the ones you did not plan.

choices.text: `mktemp` deleting the file when the process ends
choices.why: `mktemp` creates it and then has nothing more to do with it.
It decides when to stop and cleans up nothing.
